strengths: First systematic study of safety vulnerabilities specific to diffusion-based LLMs, addressing a critical gap for this emerging model class
Well-motivated vulnerability identification grounded in architecture-specific mechanisms (bidirectional modeling + parallel decoding)
Comprehensive experimental validation across 4 dLLM families and 3 major benchmarks with very strong results (up to 100% keyword-based ASR, 78.5% improvement over baselines)
Thoughtfully designed DIJA framework with multiple diversification strategies (prompt variations, masking patterns, benign separators)
Demonstrated robustness of attacks against existing defense mechanisms, highlighting urgent need for dLLM-specific defenses
Extensive reproducibility details, prompt templates, and ablation studies (generation length, masked token counts)
Clear factorization of vulnerability (Eq. 7) and insightful analysis of why defenses designed for autoregressive models fail
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in attack method itself—interleaved mask-text prompt construction via in-context learning is relatively straightforward; primary contribution is vulnerability identification rather than algorithmic innovation
Absence of white-box attacks (e.g., GCG-based variants); only black-box attacks evaluated, limiting comprehensiveness of threat model analysis
Restricted victim model coverage: only 4 dLLM families (all masked diffusion models), mostly 7-8B parameters; generalizability to other non-autoregressive architectures unclear
Insufficient analysis of solutions—paper identifies vulnerabilities but proposes no defenses; dismisses perplexity-based approaches without deep investigation; limited guidance for practitioners
Evaluation methodology concerns: no human validation, keyword-based ASR is weak metric, no false positive analysis, heavy reliance on GPT-4o as evaluator without assessing evaluation bias
Weak theoretical analysis—while Eq. 7 provides factorization, deeper formal analysis of why interleaving creates exploitability is missing; observations on Figure 6-7 lack theoretical grounding
Limited baseline comparisons: ReNeLLM is strongest baseline but designed for autoregressive models; no baselines adapted specifically for dLLMs
Missing ablations: no statistical significance testing, no human evaluation, no analysis of practical likelihood of such attacks in real deployment scenarios

strengths: First systematic investigation of safety vulnerabilities specific to diffusion-based LLMs, identifying architecture-specific weaknesses rooted in bidirectional modeling and parallel decoding
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 7 victim models, 3 benchmarks, 4 baselines, and multiple metrics with rigorous ablation studies (Table 11) demonstrating the core mechanism
Strong empirical results with up to 100% keyword-based ASR and 78.5% improvement over ReNeLLM, with high stability across runs (std < 0.7%, Table 10)
Excellent reproducibility: detailed algorithms, implementation details, stability analysis, prompt templates, mask syntax mapping, and commitment to code/model release
Rigorous evaluation methodology including human validation of harmfulness scores with >93% inter-rater agreement (Table 18) and multiple evaluation metrics to reduce bias
Thoughtful treatment of threat model assumptions and responsible disclosure practices; proposes preliminary defense strategy (Refusal-Aware Denoising Alignment) with targeted evaluation
Clear technical insight into why dLLMs are vulnerable: forced contextual coherence at masked positions fundamentally prevents refusal at inference time
weaknesses: Attack mechanism is relatively straightforward—exploiting an obvious architectural difference; ablation (Table 11) shows 54.8% ASR-e achievable with simple heuristic templates without LLM refinement, limiting novelty
Practical threat model limited for current deployments: closed-source dLLM APIs don't yet expose arbitrary mask placement; threat is prospective, not immediate

Defense solutions are preliminary and incomplete: alignment strategy requires 10k examples specifically for this attack pattern, unclear generalization to novel variations; non-negligible task performance degradation (GPQA: 32.4→27.5); no evaluation against adaptive attacks
Limited scope: exclusively focuses on text-only dLLMs; newer multi-modal models (Li et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025a) unexplored; multi-modal masking may have different safety properties
Section B.6 shows significant performance degradation under UI constraints (single mask span: 31.5% ASR-e), raising questions about real-world applicability when deployments restrict mask usage

Incomplete analysis of existing defenses: paper shows Self-reminder and RPO ineffective but doesn't deeply explain why or explore bidirectional defense strategies; no discussion of system-level detection or monitoring
Evaluation metrics have limitations: keyword-based ASR is crude; human validation on only N=100 samples; no inter-rater disagreement analysis or qualitative failure case examination

Core attack shows straightforward heuristic components (prompt diversification, benign separator insertion) without principled motivation; contribution feels somewhat incremental relative to the vulnerability identification itself
